How to fill it in

What makes a one-page case study work

A prospect reading a case study is asking, “Does this work for someone like me?” So the page should lead with the result, describe a situation they recognize and prove it with specific numbers and a real person’s words. Keep it to one page so it gets read and forwarded. The sample in this template is invented, so every sentence needs replacing.

Step 1: Get permission and the facts

Before writing, get the customer’s written agreement to be named and quoted, and ask them to approve the final text. Collect their before and after numbers. If a number is an estimate, label it as one. Never publish results the customer has not confirmed, and do not use a quote you made up.

Step 2: Write the headline last, but make it a result

The best headlines name the customer and the outcome: “[Customer] cut invoice errors by 42% in nine days”. Avoid “Success story” or “How [Customer] uses our product”. In the PowerPoint version, edit the title text directly.

Step 3: The challenge

Two to four sentences describing the situation before you: what the customer was doing, why it hurt and what it cost, with a number if you have one. Use the customer’s own words where you can. Do not mention your product yet.

Step 4: The solution

Four short bullets: what was set up, how fast, what changed for the user and what the customer now sees. Stick to facts the customer would agree with. Include the time to go live, because it answers an objection before it is raised.

Step 5: Three results

Pick three results with before and after values, for example cost, coverage and time. Write the label as a sentence, such as “reduction in approval time, from 12 days to 3 days”. The skill that made this file calculates the percentage from before and after so the headline, callouts and body cannot disagree. If you edit by hand in PowerPoint, work out each percentage yourself: (before minus after) divided by before for a reduction.

Step 6: Quote and call to action

One or two sentences from a named person with a role. Then one clear next step, a short sentence and a link or button: for example “Book a free audit”. Replace the sample URL with your own. The footer states the results are specific to this customer; keep a note like it.

Reuse

Use the PDF as an email attachment or a download on your website, and the slide inside a sales deck or a board pack. For the numbers behind a customer story, a KPI report can help you find what to highlight.

Common mistakes to avoid

The weakest case studies are vague (“improved efficiency”), hide the numbers, bury the result in the third paragraph or read like an advert. Do not exaggerate: if the customer saw a 42% reduction in one area, do not turn it into an across-the-board claim. Do not compare against a baseline the customer would not recognise. Keep sentences short, and avoid unexplained jargon. Finally, keep a record of where each figure came from and who approved it, so you can answer when a prospect asks.

Frequently asked questions

Is this case study template free?

Yes. Both files are free.

Are the results real?

No. The company, customer, quote and figures are fictional placeholders. Replace all of them with real, approved information.

Can I edit the PDF?

Edit the PowerPoint slide and export your own PDF, or use the free skill to rebuild it.

How long should a case study be?

One page works well for sales. Some teams keep a longer version too, but start with the one-pager.

Do I need the customer’s permission?

Yes. Get written approval to name them, quote them and publish the numbers.
